hints: Think about what molecule already carries a copy of the gene sequence inside a cell that is expressing that gene, and could be used as a template if you cannot get the DNA itself.
Recall which viral enzyme makes DNA from an RNA template, and contrast this biological copying route with a fully artificial route built in the laboratory.
For the artificial route, think about where scientists get the information to decide the order of nucleotides to join together, such as stored sequence data.
walkthrough:
Copying From mRNA With Reverse Transcriptase**
If the gene cannot be cut out of donor DNA, you can still copy its expressed message. Take mRNA for that protein from donor cells and use reverse transcriptase to make complementary DNA (cDNA) from it. This cDNA contains the coding sequence without introns and can be used in genetic engineering.

Building a Gene Chemically From Sequence Data**
The second method does not need any donor template at all. Look up the known amino acid or nucleotide sequence from a database, then chemically join free nucleotides together in the correct order to synthesise the gene artificially.

Linking to Three Marks**
You need any three clear points: mRNA as starting material, reverse transcriptase for cDNA, and chemical joining of nucleotides using database sequence information. That covers the two methods.

Final answer: Method 1: make cDNA from mRNA using reverse transcriptase. Method 2: chemically synthesise the gene by joining nucleotides in an order deduced from a known amino acid / nucleotide sequence from a database. Any three points for 3 marks.

hints: Start by thinking about the names - ligase sounds like ligate or join together, while polymerase sounds like polymerise or build a polymer.
Ask yourself which enzyme seals a nick between two existing DNA pieces, for example when inserting a gene into an opened plasmid.
Now ask which enzyme needs free activated nucleotides and a template to grow a new strand one nucleotide at a time.
walkthrough:
Sealing the Backbone Is Ligase Work**
DNA ligase catalyses formation of phosphodiester bonds to seal nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone. DNA polymerase does not seal two pre-made pieces together, it only adds single nucleotides to a growing chain. So row 1 is tick for ligase, cross for polymerase.

Putting a Gene Into a Plasmid Needs Sealing**
When a gene and a cut plasmid with sticky ends are mixed, hydrogen bonds form between complementary bases but the backbone is still broken. DNA ligase joins the gene to the plasmid by sealing the backbone. Polymerase is not used for this joining step. So row 2 is tick for ligase, cross for polymerase.

Extending a Chain Is Polymerase Work**
DNA polymerase adds free activated DNA nucleotides to the 3-prime end of a polynucleotide during replication, PCR and sequencing. Ligase cannot add free single nucleotides, it only joins existing polynucleotide sections. So row 3 is cross for ligase, tick for polymerase.

Final answer: Joins two sections of sugar-phosphate backbone: ligase tick, polymerase cross. Adds a gene to a plasmid: ligase tick, polymerase cross. Adds free activated DNA nucleotides to a polynucleotide: ligase cross, polymerase tick.

hints: Think of a PCR cycle as three jobs in order - first open up the double helix, then attach short starting pieces, then build new DNA.
Recall which job needs the highest near-boiling heat to break hydrogen bonds, and which needs cooling so primers can hydrogen bond stably.
Remember that the building enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium works best at a warm intermediate temperature close to its optimum.
walkthrough:
High Heat to Denature - About $95^{\circ}\text{C}$**
At $90-98^{\circ}\text{C}$ the hydrogen bonds between base pairs break and the double-stranded template DNA denatures into two single strands. This gives access for primers and nucleotides in the next steps.

Cool to Anneal Primers - About $55^{\circ}\text{C}$**
At $50-65^{\circ}\text{C}$ the mixture is cooled so primers can bind by complementary base pairing / anneal to their specific sequences on the single strands. If it stayed too hot, primers could not form stable hydrogen bonds.

Intermediate Optimum to Extend - About $72^{\circ}\text{C}$**
At $68-75^{\circ}\text{C}$ heat-stable Taq DNA polymerase has its optimum and extends from the primers, adding complementary nucleotides to synthesise new DNA strands. Each cycle therefore doubles the gene copies.

Final answer: $90-98^{\circ}\text{C}$ - DNA denatures, strands separate; $50-65^{\circ}\text{C}$ - primers anneal / base pair to DNA; $68-75^{\circ}\text{C}$ - Taq DNA polymerase synthesises new DNA strand.
